content:
There’s a familiar refrain: “always use the most expensive model.” Anthropic’s Opus 4.6, the top of the pricing pyramid.
The reasoning goes: the most expensive model is the smartest model. For any given task, the premium model nails it on the first try. A cheap model might get it wrong, require corrections, and by the time you’re done, the cumulative time and token cost has surpassed what you’d have paid for Opus upfront.
What the expensive model buys you comes at a cost though:
Expensive Slow A New Baseline
Recently I’ve been using DeepSeekV4Flash, and it’s made me rethink this. For plenty of simple tasks—tweaking Emacs config, writing throwaway Python scripts—it just works. Fast. Cheap.
Even for tasks that don’t need a human in the loop, the requirements are the same:
Correct Cheap Fast The cheap model’s capability has simply caught up to a new baseline.
But Then It Fails
Of course, the story doesn’t end there. When I used DeepSeekV4Flash to modify an OpenClaw configuration, it got it wrong. Twice. And in that moment it felt obvious: should’ve used GPT-5.5 from the start.
The Real Question
So the ability to judge task difficulty before starting would be genuinely valuable. What we currently agree are simple tasks:
(Straightforward) translation Summarization Text formatting But “simple” is slippery. Editing Emacs config looks trivial until the model doesn’t know about recent built-in changes. Translation seems easy until you hit idioms that require real cultural understanding.
The real insight isn’t that cheap models are bad, or that expensive models are always worth it. It’s that the baseline keeps shifting. Cheap models today are capable enough for a widening circle of tasks—and knowing where that circle ends is what separates good judgment from superstition.

The Old Wisdom There’s a conventional argument that goes: “Always use the most expensive model.”
The logic is straightforward — the most expensive model is also the smartest one. For any given task, the top-tier model gets it right in one shot. A cheaper model? It might fumble, need corrections, and by the time you’ve iterated, you’ve burned through more tokens and time than if you’d just picked the expensive model to begin with.
The trade-off with expensive models is obvious:
Cost — they’re pricier per call Latency — they’re slower What I’ve Been Noticing Lately My recent experience with DeepSeekV4Flash made me revisit this.
For a surprising number of mundane tasks — tweaking Emacs config, writing short Python scripts, the kind of grunt work that fills a developer’s day — the cheap model handles them just fine. And it’s fast. And it’s cheap.
A Closer Look Even for fully automated tasks, we’re optimizing for the same three things:
Correctness — the answer is right Efficiency — it doesn’t waste resources Speed — it finishes quickly What’s changed is the baseline. Cheap models have gotten good enough that they work for a widening range of jobs. The “dumb model” of last year is this year’s capable assistant.
But then there are the counterexamples. I once asked DeepSeekV4Flash to modify an OpenClaw configuration and it messed up — twice. In that moment, I would have happily paid for GPT-5.5 upfront.
This surfaces a genuinely useful skill: knowing whether a task is “simple” or “hard” before you start. Right now, the community seems to converge on a handful of safe-bet simple tasks:
Translation (the straightforward kind) Summarization Over time, this consensus will grow. We’ll get better at classification.
The Bottom Line Cheap and expensive models will carve out their own niches. The game isn’t deciding which model to use — it’s learning to tell which arena you’re walking into before you place your bet.
